name: Context Engineering: From Prompts to Corporate Multi-Agent Architecture (arXiv:2603.09619)
publisher: Vera V. Vishnyakova, affiliated with HSE University (Higher School of Economics); single-author preprint posted to arXiv, not yet confirmed peer-reviewed/published in a venue.
date_published: v1 submitted March 10, 2026; v2 revised March 13, 2026 (arXiv:2603.09619). Categories: cs.AI, cs.MA.
source_type: academic paper (conceptual/framework paper, not an empirical study)
claim_value: Argues that as AI systems move from stateless chatbots to autonomous multi-step agents, prompt engineering is 'necessary but insufficient,' and proposes context engineering (CE) as a standalone discipline covering the design, structuring, and management of an agent's entire informational environment, framed as the agent's 'operating system.' Introduces five context-quality criteria (relevance, sufficiency, isolation, economy, provenance) and, beyond CE itself, proposes two further disciplines: intent engineering (encoding organizational goals, values, and trade-off hierarchies into agent infrastructure) and specification engineering (a machine-readable corpus of corporate policies/standards enabling autonomous multi-agent operation at scale). These are combined into a four-level cumulative maturity pyramid (prompt -> context -> intent -> specification engineering), each level subsuming the one below as a necessary foundation. The paper is roughly 25 pages and cites a Deloitte 2026 figure that 75% of enterprises plan agentic AI adoption within two years, alongside a KPMG 2026 citation on enterprise agentic AI scaling challenges and references to vendor architectures (Google ADK, Anthropic, LangChain).
claim_definition: A conceptual framework/taxonomy paper, not a benchmark or empirical study: the five context-quality criteria and the three-discipline maturity pyramid (context, intent, specification engineering) are the author's own proposed classification scheme, argued from enterprise research citations (Deloitte, KPMG) and vendor architecture examples rather than from new experiments, user studies, or measured output-quality data generated by the author.
evidence_category: survey opinion / practitioner-adjacent conceptual argument, supported by secondary enterprise-survey citations (Deloitte, KPMG) rather than original empirical data
reproducibility: Not applicable in the benchmark sense: the paper presents no original experiment, dataset, or eval harness of its own to replicate. Its factual backbone (the 75% Deloitte adoption figure, the KPMG scaling-challenge point) is secondary citation of other organizations' survey data, which would need to be verified against those original reports rather than against this paper.
publisher_sells_relevant_product: No direct commercial product identified. The author is university-affiliated (HSE University) rather than vendor-affiliated, though the paper draws on, and favorably frames, vendor architectures (Google's Agent Development Kit, Anthropic, LangChain) as supporting examples; no funding disclosure or conflict-of-interest statement was located in the fetched content.
conflict_notes: No specific numerical discrepancy was found between this paper and secondary paraphrases of it (the secondary summaries checked agree closely with the abstract-level description). The main thing to flag if this is cited: the paper's own account describes enterprise agentic AI deployment as having 'surged and retreated' due to scaling complexity, which cuts against a simple 'context engineering has solved enterprise AI' reading and should be preserved if the paper is cited for its adoption-maturity argument.
relationship: Extends and complicates the 'prompt engineering is dead, context engineering is what matters now' framing rather than simply restating it: it accepts the premise that prompt engineering alone is insufficient for agentic systems, but immediately argues that context engineering itself is also insufficient at enterprise scale, needing to be subsumed by intent engineering and specification engineering. This is useful as a source that takes the 'context engineering is the new discipline' claim one step further than most of the research set, while implicitly conceding that each successive relabeling (prompt -> context -> intent -> specification) is itself an escalation of the same naming pattern already visible in the 2025 survey and the Karpathy/Lutke origin tweets.
derivative_of: Shares the same basic premise and much of the same terminology (context engineering as a discipline beyond prompting) as the July 2025 'A Survey of Context Engineering for Large Language Models' (arXiv:2507.13334) already logged in this research set, but no direct citation of that specific survey was found in the fetched content, and the two works differ in scope and method: the 2025 survey is a large multi-author literature synthesis (roughly 1,400 papers cited) covering retrieval, generation, processing, and management of context broadly across LLM systems, while this 2026 paper is a single-author conceptual paper narrowly focused on enterprise/corporate multi-agent deployment, adding the intent-engineering and specification-engineering layers that the 2025 survey does not propose. Based on available evidence this reads as independent work operating in the same research lineage and inheriting its core 'context engineering as discipline' framing, rather than being an explicit extension, response to, or formal successor of the 2025 survey.
register: primarily academic researcher and enterprise IT buyer (the paper is framed academically but its content, maturity model, and Deloitte/KPMG citations target an enterprise architecture/governance audience, not a general ML research audience).
notes: Core bibliographic facts (author, affiliation, dates, abstract, five criteria, three-discipline pyramid, Deloitte/KPMG citations, vendor references) were corroborated across the arXiv abstract page and a third-party summary (alphaxiv), but the full PDF could not be parsed as text in this session (binary/compressed stream content only), so page-level detail such as an explicit citation list, funding disclosure, or a direct citation/non-citation of arXiv:2507.13334 could not be independently confirmed from the primary PDF itself. Treat the 'no direct citation found' conclusion in derivative_of as based on secondary summaries, not a full-text citation check.
new_angle: Adds a concrete 2026 example of the 'context engineering' framing being extended one level further (into intent engineering and specification engineering) for an enterprise-governance audience, which is useful evidence for the article_ideas.md point that today's framing escalates year over year (prompt -> context -> intent -> specification) rather than settling on a stable claim. Also surfaces the paper's own 'surged and retreated' characterization of enterprise agentic AI adoption, a useful qualifier against breezier claims elsewhere in this research set that context engineering has already delivered enterprise-scale results.
